title: Intracoronary imaging to assess atherosclerosis and to guide percutaneous coronary intervention.
why: Intracoronary imaging can lower major adverse events in PCI, especially for complex lesions.
findings: Studies show that using IVUS or OCT for stent sizing and placement reduces cardiac death, MI, and repeat revascularization. The benefit is most pronounced in left-main, bifurcation, calcified, long lesions, and in acute coronary syndrome patients.
take_home: In complex coronary interventions, routinely use IVUS/OCT guidance to improve procedural success and long‑term outcomes.

title: Clinical Impact of Physiology-Guided PCI: 1-year Results of the Post-Revascularization Optimization and Physiological Evaluation of Intermediate Lesions using Fractional Flow Reserve (PROPHET-FFR) Study.
why: It shows that checking physiology after PCI can cut down future events, which matters when deciding how aggressively to treat intermediate lesions.
findings: In 1,986 patients, those who had post‑PCI physiology had a 3.4% MACE rate versus 7.6% in conventional PCI. The benefit was mainly fewer repeat procedures. The advantage held up after matching patients on baseline characteristics.
take_home: Use post‑PCI physiological assessment to guide optimization and reduce 12‑month adverse events.

title: Transseptal Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement for Mitral Annular Calcification: ENCIRCLE MAC Registry 1-Year Outcomes.
why: This study shows that transseptal TMVR can be a viable option for high‑risk patients with MAC‑related mitral disease, a group often excluded from surgery.
findings: At 1 year, 21% died and 19% were hospitalized for heart failure, giving a 33% composite rate. MR was reduced to ≤1+ in 98% of patients, and most patients had sustained symptom improvement. Stroke occurred in 5%, and valve‑related complications were seen in about 10–12%.
take_home: Transseptal TMVR with the SAPIEN M3 offers durable MR relief and symptom benefit in selected MAC patients, but it carries a substantial risk of mortality, stroke, and valve complications.

title: Intraprocedural Cardiac Arrest in Patients Undergoing Percutaneous Coronary Interventions in the United States: An Analysis of the NCDR CathPCI Registry.
why: This study tells us how often cardiac arrest happens during PCI and how deadly it is, which matters for our cath lab protocols. It also highlights risk factors like age, arrhythmias, and the need for mechanical support, so we can better anticipate and prevent these events.
findings: Intraprocedural cardiac arrest occurs in 0.93% of all PCIs, rising from 0.62% in 2018 to 1.07% in 2023. About 40.5% of those patients die in-hospital, with 45.4% of deaths occurring in the cath lab. Mortality has slightly declined over time, but remains high. Predictors include STEMI, NSTEMI, older age, ventricular arrhythmias, severe aortic stenosis, vasopressors, mechanical circulatory support, perforation, dissection, tamponade, intraprocedural heart failure or MI, and temporary pacemaker implantation.
take_home: Even though intraprocedural cardiac arrest is still rare, its mortality remains high, and recognizing the identified risk factors can guide us to tighten monitoring and early intervention during high-risk PCI.

title: Immediate Versus Staged Complete Revascularization in Multivessel Disease and STEMI: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
why: Immediate complete revascularization in STEMI with multivessel disease may raise 1‑year mortality, so staged strategy is safer.
findings: The meta‑analysis of 4 RCTs (2,651 pts) showed a 50% higher risk of all‑cause death with immediate revascularization, but a lower risk of procedural MI. No benefit was seen for spontaneous MI, cardiac death or unplanned revascularization.
take_home: In STEMI patients with multivessel disease, staged complete revascularization appears to reduce mortality compared with immediate intervention.

title: Frequency and Prognosis of Alternative Definitions of Occlusion Myocardial Infarction Across the Whole Spectrum of Acute Coronary Syndromes.
why: It shows that many ACS patients actually have occlusion MI even without ST‑elevation, which matters for risk stratification and treatment decisions.
findings: In 6,558 ACS patients, OMI prevalence varied from 38% to 76% depending on the definition. Definitions based on impaired flow (TIMI 0‑2) were linked to a 1‑year mortality risk 1.5‑2.1 times higher, while a high troponin cut‑off alone did not. Patients with NSTE‑ACS who met the flow‑based OMI definition had mortality similar to STEMI.
take_home: Use flow‑based OMI definitions to identify high‑risk ACS patients beyond ST‑elevation status and guide more aggressive therapy.

title: Occlusion-Focused Triage vs Very-High-Risk NSTEMI Criteria: A DIFOCCULT-3 Substudy.
why: It shows that an occlusion-focused triage picks up more patients for early invasive care, which could change how we manage NSTEMI without diagnostic STE.
findings: The OMI/NOMI strategy led to 45.4% of patients getting invasive management within 2 hours versus 13.6% with the standard STEMI/NSTEMI approach. Adjudicated acute coronary occlusion was identified in 35.1% versus 16.7% of patients, and angiographic yield was unchanged.
take_home: Using an occlusion-focused diagnostic approach may enable earlier invasive treatment and better detection of occlusion without lowering angiographic success.

title: Acute Coronary Occlusions in NSTEMI Undergoing Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: Insights From the CathPCI Registry.
why: A large registry shows that a notable fraction of NSTEMI patients actually have acute occlusions, which puts them at higher risk for shock and arrhythmias, so we should be alert to early reperfusion.
findings: In over 1.1 million PCI cases, 11% of NSTEMI had acute occlusion. Those patients had higher rates of cardiogenic shock (3.8% vs 1.9%), ventricular arrhythmias (2.0% vs 1.3%) and cardiac arrest (2.7% vs 1.6%) and a 2.3‑fold higher odds of the composite in‑hospital outcome compared with NSTEMI without occlusion.
take_home: NSTEMI patients with acute occlusion represent a high‑risk group that may benefit from earlier reperfusion to improve in‑hospital outcomes.

title: Accelerated 3D Late Gadolinium Enhancement Pulse Sequence with Isotropic Spatial Resolution, Self-Navigation of Respiratory Motion, and Arrhythmia Rejection for Quantification of Left Atrial Fibrosis in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation.
why: It shows a new 3‑D LGE sequence that can reliably image the thin left atrium in AF patients, which could help us better assess fibrosis before ablation.
findings: The 1.5 mm³ isotropic sequence produced acceptable image quality in all patients, and arrhythmia rejection improved contrast and sharpness. Fibrosis burden was higher in repeat‑ablation patients compared to controls, but similar to first‑time ablation patients.
take_home: This technique offers a practical, high‑resolution way to quantify left‑atrial fibrosis at 1.5 T, potentially aiding patient selection for ablation.

title: Diffuse elevations of T1 and T2 are common in newly transplanted pediatric cardiac grafts without rejection and decrease over time.
why: Early post‑transplant CMR often shows elevated T1/T2 due to ischemia‑reperfusion injury, not rejection. Using graft‑age‑specific norms can prevent false‑positive rejection diagnoses.
findings: New grafts (≤6 mo) had higher mean T1 (≈27 ms) and peak T1 (≈43 ms) and mean T2 (≈2.6 ms) compared with established grafts. Diastolic function trends were worse in new grafts, with lower left‑atrial strain and larger volumes, though not statistically significant. Over time, T1 values trended toward normalization in the few patients followed longitudinally.
take_home: In the first six months after pediatric heart transplant, diffuse T1/T2 elevations and transient diastolic impairment are expected; use graft‑age‑specific reference ranges to avoid mistaking these changes for rejection.

title: Sex-Based Differences in Chronic Heart Failure: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
why: Women are still underrepresented in heart‑failure trials, which matters for our ICU patients who often have HF.
findings: Only about 27% of participants in drug trials and 25% in device trials were women. Women were less represented in HFrEF trials than HFpEF trials. In drug trials, women seemed to gain slightly more relative benefit from therapy, while device trials showed no clear sex interaction.
take_home: Future heart‑failure studies should enroll more women and analyze sex‑specific outcomes, as women may derive greater benefit from pharmacologic therapy.

title: 4D Flow Acquisition Parameters as Technical Correlates of Hemodynamic Measurements: An Analysis of the multicenter Tetralogy of Fallot Registry of 4D flow Energetics and Kinetics (TREK).
why: It shows that 4D flow CMR biomarkers vary with acquisition settings, so you need to consider image quality when interpreting flow data.
findings: In a 345‑patient registry, sequence type, field strength, voxel size, temporal resolution, and VENC all affected signal‑to‑noise and velocity‑to‑noise ratios, and aliasing. Lower aSNR was linked to higher measured kinetic energy, vorticity, and viscous loss, especially for vorticity and viscous loss, while kinetic energy was more stable.
take_home: When using 4D flow CMR in repaired TOF, standardize acquisition parameters and monitor aSNR, aVNR, and aliasing to ensure reliable hemodynamic biomarkers.

title: Evaluating the Role of Lower Extremity Elastic Bandage in Patients with Acute Decompensated Heart Failure.
why: If diuretic resistance is a nightmare in ADHF, a simple elastic bandage might help you squeeze more out of the loop diuretics.
findings: In 176 ICU patients, applying elastic bandages lowered the daily furosemide dose by about 1.2 mg per 40‑mg equivalent and boosted diuretic efficiency by roughly 340 mL per 40‑mg dose, without changing urine output or mortality.
take_home: Elastic leg compression could be a low‑cost adjunct to improve diuretic response in ADHF, but randomized trials are needed to confirm benefit.

title: Impact of the Extent, Pattern, and Location of Replacement Myocardial Fibrosis on Clinical Outcomes in Aortic Regurgitation.
why: It shows how CMR findings can flag AR patients at higher risk of heart failure events, which matters for deciding when to intervene.
findings: About half of chronic AR patients had LGE, and those with more than 2.6% of the myocardium scarred were at higher risk of major events. A subendocardial‑involved pattern further increased that risk, even after accounting for scar size.
take_home: In aortic regurgitation, LGE extent >2.6% plus a subendocardial pattern identifies patients who need closer monitoring or earlier surgical consideration.

title: Identifying the High-Risk Arrhythmic Mitral Valve Prolapse Phenotype by Imaging.
why: This review shows that advanced imaging, especially CMR, can identify the high‑risk arrhythmic MVP phenotype that is otherwise hard to spot, which is crucial for preventing sudden death in young women.
findings: CMR detects replacement fibrosis with late gadolinium enhancement and diffuse fibrosis with T1 mapping, even when LGE is absent. Baseline ECG and echo identify MVP and exclude severe regurgitation; exercise stress and prolonged monitoring can reveal PVC triggers. Machine‑learning models that combine annular disjunction, fibrosis extent, and location outperform symptom‑based risk scores.
take_home: Use multimodality imaging and rhythm monitoring to risk‑stratify patients with mitral valve prolapse before any mitral intervention.

title: "Baseline Characteristics and Utilization of Medical Therapies in Acute Hospitalized and Chronic Heart Failure Patients Enrolled in GRASP-HF: Differences Between ICARe-HF and Non-ICARe-HF Centres".
why: It shows that ICARe‑HF accredited centres use guideline‑directed therapy more often, especially in HFrEF, which could improve patient care.
findings: In a cohort of 10,936 patients, those treated at ICARe‑HF centres were older, had more comorbidities but less congestion. They achieved higher rates of quadruple GDMT, particularly ARNI and SGLT2 inhibitors, and had a lower crude in‑hospital mortality that disappeared after adjustment.
take_home: Accreditation seems to drive better guideline adherence, especially for HFrEF, but the mortality benefit remains uncertain.

title: Underserved communities at risk of heart failure: effectiveness of community-based recruitment strategies and burden of unrecognised cardiovascular disease.
why: It shows that community‑based recruitment can uncover a high burden of hidden CVD in underserved groups, which matters for early HF prevention.
findings: About 23% of participants had actionable cardiac findings, including 9% with previously unrecognised MI, 60% with uncontrolled BP, and 30% with elevated NT‑proBNP. Primary‑care and digital outreach recruited 81% and 12% of the cohort, respectively, at a low cost.
take_home: Targeted primary‑care and digital outreach can efficiently identify high‑risk underserved patients, revealing a substantial hidden burden of CVD that could be addressed early to prevent heart failure.

title: Automatic 3D TOF-MRA Intracranial Aneurysm Segmentation using SAM-Guided Multi-View Decoding Network.
why: Not relevant to cardiology practice, focuses on brain aneurysm imaging.
findings: A deep‑learning model segmented intracranial aneurysms on 3D TOF‑MRA with about 86% sensitivity and 0.88 Dice score internally, and 83% sensitivity and 0.84 Dice externally. It outperformed junior radiologists and matched mid‑level ones, processing each scan in roughly 72 seconds.
take_home: This AI tool shows promise for rapid, accurate aneurysm detection on MRA, but has no direct impact on cardiac care.

title: The Prognostic Value of Entropy from T1 Mapping in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension.
why: It shows a new CMR metric that could help us risk‑stratify PAH patients better than we currently do.
findings: Higher LV entropy on T1 mapping was linked to worse biomarkers, more RV dysfunction, and higher mortality. It independently predicted death and improved ESC risk models. The cut‑offs were about 8.6 for entropy and 8.3 for entropy without IPs.
take_home: LV entropy from CMR is a useful, independent prognostic marker in PAH that adds value to existing ESC risk scores.

title: Cardiovascular effects of continued vs. discontinued anabolic-androgenic steroid use: a longitudinal follow-up study.
why: It shows that anabolic steroids can cause LV hypertrophy and systolic dysfunction, but stopping them can reverse the damage—important for drug‑induced cardiomyopathy.
findings: Continued users had higher LV mass, lower EF and worse diastolic function. Discontinuing steroids reduced LV mass and improved EF, bringing values close to non‑users. Antihypertensive therapy helped improve EF in ongoing users.
take_home: Stopping anabolic steroids reverses LV remodeling and improves function; antihypertensives may benefit those who continue use.

title: Open Visiting Policy and Delirium in Adult Patients in ICUs: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
why: Delirium is common in cardiac ICU patients and can worsen outcomes, so knowing that family presence helps may improve care.
findings: Open/flexible visiting cuts delirium risk by about half and shortens mechanical‑ventilation by roughly 0.4 days. It doesn’t change ICU stay, infection rates or mortality.
take_home: Allowing families to visit more freely in the cardiac ICU can reduce delirium and ventilation time without harming other outcomes.

title: Developing Models for Complicated Outcomes in Acutely Intoxicated ICU Patients With and Without Toxicity Information.
why: Even though it's not a cardiac study, the models could help us triage ICU patients with intoxication, many of whom may develop cardiac complications. Knowing the predictors could improve our bedside decisions.
findings: They built two models: one with lab values, one with a toxicity score. The lab model had AUROC 0.79, the toxicity model 0.77. The toxicity score only mattered when labs were missing. Both models were well calibrated.
take_home: Use the lab-based model when you have labs; otherwise the toxicity score can guide decisions in intoxicated ICU patients.

title: Association of Tele-Critical Care Capability With Interhospital Transfers and Potentially Low-Value Transfers Among Critically Ill Medicare Beneficiaries.
why: Tele‑critical care could change how we decide to transfer critically ill cardiac patients, potentially reducing unnecessary moves and improving early post‑transfer outcomes.
findings: Hospitals with tele‑critical care were slightly more likely to transfer patients (aOR 1.08), yet those transferred had lower early death/hospice rates (4.6% vs 6.6%) and were more often discharged home within two days (4.7% vs 3.7%).
take_home: Tele‑critical care modestly increases transfer rates but improves early post‑transfer outcomes, suggesting better transfer selection for critically ill patients.

title: Ventilatory Management in Neurocritical Versus Non-Neurocritical Care Patients: A Pooled Analysis From the PRIME Database.
why: It’s not directly about heart disease, but ICU ventilatory strategies can affect cardiac patients, so it’s worth a quick glance.
findings: Neurocritical patients were ventilated with lower tidal volumes, lower driving pressures, lower mechanical power, and higher compliance compared with non‑neurocritical patients. They developed ARDS more often (8.7% vs 3.9%) but had lower ICU mortality (14.3% vs 22.8%). Among neurocritical patients who got ARDS, lower tidal volume and higher FiO₂, driving pressure and mechanical power were seen, and tidal volume per predicted body weight independently predicted ARDS.
take_home: In neuro‑ICU patients, using lower tidal volumes and driving pressures may reduce ARDS risk, yet these patients still face higher ARDS rates but better survival than non‑neuro‑ICU patients.

title: Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Ventilation Rates and Outcomes.
why: It suggests that the standard 20-30 breaths/min may not be optimal for pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest, especially in kids under 8, which could influence resuscitation protocols in the ICU.
findings: Out of 234 events, only 37% had ventilation rates in the guideline range. No overall survival benefit was seen with guideline rates. In children under 8, rates ≥26 breaths/min were linked to better survival. The study calls for further research to confirm these thresholds.
take_home: Consider revising pediatric CPR ventilation targets, particularly for children under 8, as higher rates may improve survival.

title: Association of Oliguria With Acute Kidney Injury, Chronic Kidney Disease, and Mortality: Determining the Optimal Threshold in Critically Ill Patients.
why: In the ICU, especially with cardiogenic shock or MCS, early kidney injury can worsen outcomes, so knowing precise urine output cutoffs matters.
findings: The study found that urine output thresholds as low as 0.16–0.53 mL/kg/hr over 3–24 h predict AKI, CKD, and 90‑day death, lower than the current <0.5 mL/kg/hr definition.
take_home: Consider adopting lower oliguria thresholds to flag kidney injury earlier and potentially improve ICU care.

title: Long-Lasting Mental Disorders in Caregivers of ICU Sepsis Survivors and Their Association With Patients' Post-Intensive Care Syndrome: A Prospective Multicenter Cohort Study.
why: Mental health of ICU caregivers can influence patient recovery and overall ICU outcomes, so it’s worth knowing how common it is and what drives it.
findings: About 43% of caregivers had long‑lasting mental disorders that stayed stable over a year. The presence of mental post‑ICU syndrome in patients was strongly linked to caregiver mental problems, while physical or cognitive patient impairments were not.
take_home: Treating patients’ mental post‑ICU symptoms may also help protect caregivers’ mental health.

title: Prophylactic high-flow nasal oxygen vs. conventional oxygen for prevention of postoperative respiratory complications: a randomized trial.
why: It shows HFNC can cut postoperative respiratory problems in older lung‑surgery patients, which might be useful when we manage cardiac patients with pulmonary issues after surgery.
findings: HFNC lowered the severity of postoperative pulmonary complications and the rate of moderate‑to‑severe events. Patients on HFNC had fewer clinically relevant complications and reported better early respiratory symptoms. There was no difference in physiological measures or length of stay.
take_home: HFNC may benefit older or higher‑risk patients after lung resection, but routine prophylactic use for all patients is not warranted.

title: Machine Learning Integration of Ablation Quality Metrics for Predicting Atrial Fibrillation Recurrence: A Multicenter Study.
why: It shows a high‑accuracy ML model that uses real‑time ablation data to predict AF recurrence, which could help us tailor ablation strategies and follow‑up.
findings: The XGBoost model reached an AUC of 0.918 internally and 0.992/0.951 in two external centers, far better than clinical features alone (AUC 0.588). It identified 16.5% of patients with recurrence within a year.
take_home: Using ablation quality metrics in a ML framework gives a reliable tool to forecast AF recurrence and could inform intraprocedural decisions.

title: Long-Term Safety and Procedural Performance of an Interatrial Shunt for Heart Failure According to Ejection Fraction.
why: It shows that an interatrial shunt can be safely implanted in HFrEF patients, but not in HFpEF, which matters when considering new HF therapies.
findings: In 605 patients, 369 shunts were implanted with a 99.7% success rate and 99.4% patency at 2 years. No device‑related major events occurred. In HFrEF the shunt lowered serious adverse events, while in HFpEF it increased major events, bleeding and renal decline.
take_home: Interatrial shunting is durable and safe in HFrEF but should be avoided in HFpEF due to higher adverse events.

title: Occupational Disparities in Cardiovascular Risk and Management in Contemporary China.
why: It shows how job type and region affect heart risk, so we can tailor prevention in our ICU patients.
findings: About 1.3% of employees had CHD, higher in the north and in heavy‑industry jobs, while tech‑service workers had the lowest risk. Treatment rates for hypertension and diabetes were low (≈30% and 37%).
take_home: Occupational and geographic factors drive cardiovascular risk—targeted prevention could reduce burden in high‑risk groups.

title: Cellular consequences of non-ablative radiotherapy, a novel approach to ventricular tachycardias.
why: It shows how radiotherapy might alter ion channels and conduction, which could be relevant when considering non-invasive VT ablation options.
findings: In mice, a single 25 Gy dose increased fast and late sodium currents, raised action potential amplitude and duration, and made early afterdepolarizations more likely. It also lowered calcium handling and raised reactive oxygen species. A lower 15 Gy dose had similar but milder effects.
take_home: Radiotherapy can modify sodium channel activity and conduction, potentially suppressing VT but also risking arrhythmia and contractile dysfunction.

title: Prospective Cardiac MRI study comparing Recovered COVID-19 patients with Recovered Non-COVID-19 Viral Respiratory Infection Patients (R-COVID-CMR).
why: This study tells us that COVID‑19 doesn’t seem to leave more lingering heart inflammation than other viral infections, which is reassuring for our post‑COVID patients.
findings: They followed 152 patients with CMR at 2 weeks, 3 months, and 12 months. At every time point, the COVID and non‑COVID groups had similar heart function, T1/T2 values, extracellular volume, and late gadolinium enhancement. Blood markers were also comparable. Overall, no significant differences were seen.
take_home: In short, COVID‑19 doesn’t appear to cause worse myocardial inflammation than other viral respiratory illnesses, so we can be less alarmed about long‑term cardiac sequelae in recovered patients.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment and cardiovascular outcomes following aortic valve replacement: a nationwide observational study.
why: GLP‑1 agonists might cut mortality and rehospitalisation after valve surgery, which matters for post‑AVR care
findings: In a Danish cohort, GLP‑1 users had a 31% lower risk of death, heart‑failure admission or re‑operation over about five years. The benefit was seen for each component separately.
take_home: Consider GLP‑1 agonists as a potential strategy to improve long‑term outcomes after AVR.

title: Calcium Density as a Marker of Coronary Plaque Stabilization in Primary Prevention: The CAUGHT-CAD Trial.
why: It tells us how statins change plaque composition in people who haven’t had a heart attack yet, which is key for deciding on primary prevention strategies.
findings: Statin‑treated patients had more intermediate‑ and high‑density calcium and less non‑calcified plaque. Those with ≥30% LDL‑C drop gained even more high‑ and very high‑density calcium.
take_home: Statins not only lower LDL‑C but also shift plaque toward a denser, more stable phenotype in asymptomatic, intermediate‑risk patients.

title: Optimizing Echocardiographic Evaluation of Chronic Mitral Regurgitation: Comparison With Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Implications for Guideline Recommendations.
why: It shows how well echo criteria match CMR, the gold standard, so you can trust echo more and cut down on extra tests.
findings: Exact echo‑CMR agreement was only 51%, but 89% agreed within one grade. Specific echo signs—pulmonary vein reversal, enlarged LV with normal function, large PVSA radius, and wide vena contracta—had 80‑88% specificity for severe MR. Using fewer than four ASE criteria cut the need for full quantification from 86% to 59%.
take_home: A few key ASE signs are highly specific for severe MR, so you can often skip extensive quantification and still diagnose accurately.

title: Coexistance of Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity and Orthostatic Hypotension in Patients with Unexplained Syncope.
why: If a patient comes in with unexplained fainting, it turns out that carotid sinus hypersensitivity and orthostatic hypotension often go hand-in-hand, so you might need to look for both.
findings: About a third of the 1,900 patients had orthostatic hypotension and 17% had carotid sinus hypersensitivity. CSH was twice as common in those with OH. Nearly half of the CSH patients also had OH, and asystole during carotid massage was more frequent in the OH group.
take_home: In patients over 40 with unexplained syncope, perform both carotid sinus massage and tilt testing because the two conditions frequently coexist and can unmask a cardioinhibitory reflex.

title: A Quality Improvement Initiative to Achieve Provincial Implementation of a Web-Based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) Survey to Inform Patient-Centered Care.
why: This study shows how a web‑based family satisfaction survey can be rolled out across many ICUs, but the low completion rates highlight challenges in gathering family feedback—something to keep in mind when considering quality metrics in our cardiac ICU.
findings: They generated 24,679 keys for 353,400 admissions, but only 7,542 surveys met the 70% completion threshold—about 2% of all ICU encounters. The average satisfaction scores were high (FS‑TOTAL 86.5). Staff‑Provided keys had the highest activation rate.
take_home: Family satisfaction surveys can be implemented widely, but engagement remains low; improving activation and completion is key to meaningful data.

title: ICU Physical Environments Used for Family Conferences: A Multimodal Qualitative Evaluation with ICU Team Members.
why: This study focuses on ICU family‑conference spaces, not on cardiology‑specific care or interventions.
findings: They examined 17 spaces across four ICUs and interviewed 23 staff; staff favored dedicated rooms for privacy and fewer interruptions, noting that proximity to the patient, flexible furniture, and a calm, nonclinical atmosphere support better communication.
take_home: Improving ICU physical design can enhance the quality of family‑clinician communication during critical care discussions.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of NT-proBNP thresholds in Dyspneic Patients in the Emergency Department according to patients' characteristics: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
why: In the ED, deciding whether a dyspneic patient has acute heart failure can change management, and NT‑proBNP thresholds are the main tool we use.
findings: A single cut‑off of ≤300 ng/L rules out AHF with >97 % sensitivity and a 97 % NPV, but its specificity is only 46 %. Age‑adjusted cut‑offs (≥450, ≥900, ≥1800 ng/L for <50, 50‑75, ≥75 yrs) raise specificity to 82 % while keeping sensitivity around 86 % (AUC 0.84). In CKD and obesity the performance drops somewhat, but age‑adjusted thresholds still perform better than a fixed cut‑off.
take_home: Use ≤300 ng/L to confidently rule out acute heart failure in the ED, and apply age‑dependent thresholds to improve diagnostic accuracy when you need to rule in the disease.

title: Left Ventricular Filling Pressure Classification by Electrocardiogram, Echocardiography, and Catheterization: Prognostic Implications.
why: It shows that an AI‑enabled ECG can flag high filling pressures and predict death better than the gold‑standard catheter measurement, so you can risk‑stratify patients non‑invasively.
findings: In 4,168 patients, AI‑ECG identified elevated LVFP in 2,383, echo in 1,643, PAWP in 1,841. AI‑ECG had an AUC of 0.88 against echo and 0.71 against PAWP. Over 7.7 years, AI‑ECG‑positive patients had a 1.8‑fold higher mortality risk, echo 1.7‑fold, PAWP only 1.2‑fold.
take_home: Use AI‑ECG to screen for high LV filling pressures and prognosticate outcomes, especially when invasive hemodynamics are not feasible.

title: Multi-center study of CMR versus cardiac catheterization with endomyocardial biopsy for pediatric transplant surveillance: study protocol.
why: It could change how we monitor rejection in kids, cutting down on painful biopsies.
findings: This paper just describes the design of a multicenter trial that will compare CMR and blood biomarkers to the current gold‑standard EMB. No data yet.
take_home: Once completed, the study may give us a non‑invasive way to spot rejection early and spare patients the biopsy.

title: Radiation Vasculopathy of the Coronary Arteries: State-of-the Art Review.
why: Radiation therapy is common in thoracic cancers, and survivors are at higher risk of accelerated coronary disease that can mimic typical CAD. Being aware helps in early detection and tailored management.
findings: RACAD is driven by radiation dose and proximity of coronary arteries, with younger age and other cardiovascular risk factors amplifying risk. Symptoms can appear within 1–2 years after high‑dose exposure or after 5–20 years with lower doses. Diagnosis and treatment follow standard CAD guidelines but must account for cancer‑specific issues such as planned surgeries, bleeding risk, and cardiotoxic drugs. Prevention hinges on precision radiotherapy and cardiac shielding.
take_home: In patients who have had thoracic radiotherapy, consider RACAD as a likely culprit for coronary symptoms and integrate cancer‑specific factors into CAD care and surveillance.

title: Pyrophosphatase 2 Deficiency: Clinical Presentation, Diagnosis and Management.
why: This paper shows that a rare mitochondrial enzyme defect can cause sudden cardiac arrest in children and teens after viral illness or alcohol, a scenario we often see in the ICU.
findings: The authors compiled data on 93 patients from 53 families, including 14 previously unreported cases. All presentations were acute, with symptoms such as fatigue, vomiting, seizures and collapse, and many required CPR and arrhythmia management. The condition carries a high mortality rate, especially after viral infections in young children or alcohol exposure in teens. They also outlined current emergency and long‑term treatment protocols and highlighted the strong inheritance pattern.
take_home: Early recognition of PPA2 deficiency and implementation of specific emergency protocols can reduce mortality in this high‑risk population.

title: Standardization of Collected Biobank Data to Facilitate Cardiovascular Research: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association.
why: Standardizing biobank data can make cardiovascular research faster and more reliable, which ultimately helps us find better treatments for our patients.
findings: Large biobanks that link phenotypic data to biological samples are already proving useful for studying disease mechanisms and outcomes. However, they often collect data in a nonuniform way, limiting their usefulness. This statement reviews the current state of biobanks, endorses their use for discovery and implementation science, and outlines ways to harmonize data collection to unlock new research opportunities.
take_home: Harmonizing biobank data collection will boost the quality and impact of cardiovascular research, paving the way for new therapies.

title: ICare-FASTER (Improving Care by Faster Risk Stratification Through Use of High-Sensitivity Point-of-Care Troponin in Patients Presenting With Possible Acute Coronary Syndrome in the Emergency Department): A Stepped-Wedge Cluster-Randomized Trial.
why: Using bedside high‑sensitivity troponin cuts ED stay by almost an hour without raising 30‑day events, so we can move patients faster and free up beds.
findings: In a stepped‑wedge cluster RCT at six sites, point‑of‑care hs‑cTnI reduced median ED length of stay by 47 minutes (13 % shorter). The 30‑day myocardial infarction or cardiac death rate was identical (0.39 %) in both groups. The intervention was safe and effective.
take_home: Implement bedside high‑sensitivity troponin in the ED to safely shorten stays by nearly an hour, improving throughput without compromising patient safety.

title: Cardiovascular Genetic Counseling Is Associated With Improved Patient-Reported Outcomes Across Clinical Indications and Settings.
why: Genetic counseling can change how patients feel about their inherited heart conditions, which matters for how we manage them.
findings: In a multicenter survey of 890 adults, counseling raised empowerment scores and lowered worry and cardiac fear, even before genetic test results were known. The strength of the counselor‑patient alliance was linked to larger gains in empowerment.
take_home: Offering structured genetic counseling to patients with inherited cardiomyopathies or channelopathies improves their psychological well‑being and may support better clinical engagement.

title: Visualization of post-STEMI myocardial infarction and microvascular obstruction with non-contrast, free-breathing whole- heart iT2prep-IR BOOST.
why: A fast, contrast‑free CMR could save time and avoid gadolinium in patients who can’t tolerate it.
findings: The 3‑minute free‑breathing iT2prep‑IR BOOST scan matched LGE for infarct size and MVO detection (100% sensitivity for MVO) and its MVO volume predicted adverse LV remodeling at 1 year.
take_home: iT2prep‑IR BOOST shows promise as a rapid, non‑contrast alternative to LGE for MI and MVO assessment, but larger studies are needed to confirm its clinical utility.

title: Management of Heart transplant recipients for the non Heart Transplant health care provider. A Clinical Consensus Statement of the Heart Failure Association (HFA) and the Association of Cardiovascular Nursing & Allied Professions (ACNAP) of the ESC.
why: Many cardiologists now see heart‑transplant patients outside transplant centers; this consensus gives practical guidance on immunosuppression, rejection, infection, and long‑term complications.
findings: The statement outlines a time‑based care framework, details immunosuppressive monitoring, early rejection detection, infection prevention, and surveillance for graft vasculopathy, malignancy, CKD, and metabolic issues. It also covers fertility, surgery, rehab, palliative care, and stresses shared‑care models and early referral triggers.
take_home: Non‑transplant cardiologists should adopt this structured framework to safely manage HTx patients and coordinate timely referrals to transplant centers.

title: Decision volume and temporal workload structure as dissociable correlates of fatigue and mood in intensive care physicians: a real-time observational study.
why: It shows how the sheer number of decisions and their timing can drain ICU doctors, which could spill over into patient care in the cardiac ICU.
findings: When doctors made more decisions per 5‑minute block, they reported higher fatigue at shift end. A more bursty, clustered decision pattern was linked to better mood, while a steady, quiet shift led to mood worsening over the day.
take_home: Keeping decision loads balanced and avoiding long, flat stretches may help ICU clinicians stay mentally sharp and improve care quality.

title: Infections Acquired in the ICU Among Cancer and Other Immunosuppressed Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
why: ICU infections can complicate cardiac patients, especially those who are immunosuppressed, and may affect their outcomes.
findings: Patients with hematologic cancers or other immunosuppressive conditions had about a 1.6‑fold higher risk of ICU‑acquired infections compared to non‑immunosuppressed patients, while solid tumors did not show a significant difference.
take_home: In the ICU, immunosuppression—particularly hematologic malignancies—significantly raises infection risk, highlighting the importance of aggressive infection prevention in these patients.

title: Comparison of Drug-Coated Versus Conventional Balloons for the Side Branches of Bifurcation Lesions: OCVC-BIF Study.
why: It shows a new way to reduce side‑branch restenosis after bifurcation stenting, which could change how we approach these lesions.
findings: In 299 patients, the drug‑coated balloon arm had a 8.1% restenosis rate versus 18.3% with conventional balloons, yet 12‑month major adverse events were similar (10.1% vs 12.4%).
take_home: Adding a drug‑coated balloon to the side branch after main‑vessel stenting cuts restenosis without increasing 12‑month MACE.

title: Familial hypercholesterolaemia and thymic ageing in a Chinese cohort.
why: It links high LDL to accelerated thymic ageing, suggesting early statin use may preserve immune function and reduce long‑term cardiovascular risk.
findings: FH patients had fewer CD4+ recent thymic emigrants, especially young adults and those with pathogenic LDLR variants. Thymic output was lower and T‑cell repertoires were skewed. Statin‑treated patients, especially women, showed higher RTE levels.
take_home: Early statin therapy may help preserve thymic output in FH, underscoring the broader benefits of lipid lowering beyond plaque regression.

title: Long-Term Outcome Following Idiopathic Ventricular Fibrillation and Potential Emerging Etiologies.
why: It shows that IVF patients live long but keep having arrhythmias and that many actually have a hidden cause that can be treated.
findings: Only 3.3% died, but 52.7% had arrhythmia recurrences over 10 years. Two‑thirds of patients were later re‑classified with a specific etiology—focal, micro‑structural or inherited. Quinidine worked well for focal cases, beta‑blockers for micro‑structural ones, and ablation stopped arrhythmias in 76% of treated patients.
take_home: Most IVF survivors have low mortality but a high, persistent recurrence risk that can be mitigated by identifying the underlying cause and using targeted drugs or ablation.

title: Deep Learning-Based 3D CT Body Composition Is Associated With Mortality in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
why: It shows that automated CT body‑composition metrics can refine risk prediction for TAVR patients, which matters for peri‑operative planning.
findings: Patients with low subcutaneous fat and high fat attenuation had higher mortality, while those with more skeletal muscle and higher muscle attenuation survived better. Adding these measures raised Harrell C from 0.66 to 0.71.
take_home: Use automated 3‑D CT body‑composition analysis to improve mortality risk stratification in TAVR candidates.

title: Multimodal KCNQ1 Variant-Effect Maps Define Ion Channel Mechanisms and Disease Risk.
why: It gives a huge functional map of KCNQ1 variants, so you can better interpret genetic tests for long‑QT and arrhythmia risk.
findings: They tested 13,403 KCNQ1 variants, finding 1,757 likely pathogenic and 6,660 likely benign. Loss‑of‑function variants were linked to QT prolongation and long‑QT syndrome, and dominant‑negative variants carried a higher arrhythmia risk than simple haploinsufficiency.
take_home: This atlas lets us translate KCNQ1 genetic findings into real‑world arrhythmia risk, sharpening precision medicine for long‑QT patients.

title: Prognostic Value of Late Gadolinium Enhancement Findings in Isolated Left Ventricular Dilatation and Dilated Cardiomyopathy.
why: It shows that CMR LGE patterns give extra risk info in dilated hearts, beyond what we get from LVEF alone.
findings: Patients with LGE had higher mortality, especially when the scar was larger, in multiple spots, or located in the septum. The LGE score predicted 10‑year death with an AUC of 0.79.
take_home: In DCM and isolated LV dilatation, LGE extent, distribution, and septal location are strong, independent predictors of death and should be factored into risk stratification.

title: Patient-Level Perivascular Adipose Tissue Density Aggregation and Plaque Progression: Plaque-Free vs Plaque-Adjacent Segments.
why: It shows that perivascular fat density, especially in plaque‑free segments, could be a useful marker of plaque growth, which matters for risk stratification in coronary disease.
findings: In 412 patients, higher baseline PVAT density in the proximal RCA, whole coronary tree, and plaque‑free areas predicted greater overall plaque volume progression, but only plaque‑free PVAT predicted non‑calcified plaque growth. Changes in these PVAT measures over time also tracked plaque progression.
take_home: Plaque‑free perivascular fat density appears to be the most reliable imaging biomarker for detecting and monitoring coronary plaque progression.

title: Electromechanical Window Negativity and Arrhythmic Risk in Arrhythmogenic Mitral Valve Prolapse.
why: This study shows that a simple echo‑derived metric, EMW, can flag MVP patients at high risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmias, which is relevant for risk stratification in our ICU.
findings: EMW was markedly negative in MVP patients with sustained arrhythmias, with an AUC of 0.82. A cutoff of -30 ms gave 71% sensitivity and 83% specificity. EMW added predictive value beyond QTc and QAoCc.
take_home: Measure EMW in MVP patients; a negative value beyond -30 ms flags those at high arrhythmic risk and may guide closer monitoring or early intervention.

title: Geographic differences in outcomes after emergency surgery in nonagenarians and centenarians admitted to intensive care in Australia: a population-based study.
why: It shows that where a patient lives can affect long-term survival after ICU discharge, even when in-hospital outcomes are similar.
findings: ICU and in-hospital death rates were similar for metropolitan and regional/remote patients, but those from regional/remote areas had a 13% higher risk of dying within five years after discharge. The same pattern was not seen in elective surgery patients.
take_home: Post-discharge follow-up and support should be intensified for elderly ICU survivors from regional or remote areas to improve long-term outcomes.

title: Toward targeted assessment of inspiratory muscle weakness before extubation: a pooled individual patient data analysis from multiple observational cohorts in critically ill ventilated patients.
why: In cardiogenic shock patients on prolonged ventilation, knowing who’s at risk of extubation failure can guide timing and support strategies.
findings: Among 494 ICU patients, only low maximal inspiratory pressure (≤30 cmH₂O) after >5 days of ventilation was linked to higher extubation failure (33% vs 14%). Other tests (MEP, PCF, MRC) didn’t show significant associations.
take_home: Assess inspiratory muscle strength selectively in patients ventilated long‑term to better predict extubation success.

title: Fatigue, Anxiety and Depression 12 Months After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Population Based Cohort Study.
why: Because post‑cardiac arrest patients often suffer lingering fatigue, anxiety and depression that can impair recovery and return to work.
findings: About one‑third of survivors report fatigue, a fifth anxiety and a sixth depression at 12 months. Those with more symptoms have worse quality of life and functional outcomes. Younger age, prior mental health issues, diabetes and non‑shockable arrest raise risk, while EMS‑witnessed arrest lowers it.
take_home: Screen for and address fatigue, anxiety and depression in OHCA survivors to improve long‑term recovery.

title: Regional implementation of a prehospital advanced life support program with video-assisted physician direction and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
why: It shows how a prehospital video‑guided ALS program affects early arrest outcomes, which matters when we hand over patients to the ICU.
findings: The program raised prehospital ROSC by about 1.3 percentage points and added roughly 4 minutes to the pre‑hospital interval, but it didn’t improve survival to discharge or neurological status.
take_home: Video‑guided prehospital ALS boosts early ROSC but doesn’t change ultimate survival or brain outcomes, so its benefit for ICU care is limited.

title: Association Between Capnographic Changes During Pulse Checks of Varying Durations and Clinical Outcomes During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Multicenter Study From Türkiye (CaPTuRe).
why: Shorter pulse checks during CPR seem to improve capnographic signals and increase the chance of ROSC, which matters for ICU resuscitation practice.
findings: Patients with pulse checks ≤5 s had higher ETCO2 values, lower loss rates, faster recovery times, and a 2.4‑fold higher odds of ROSC compared with checks lasting 6‑10 s.
take_home: Aim for pulse checks under 5 seconds during CPR to enhance capnographic dynamics and improve ROSC rates.

title: Identifying the Operational Bottleneck to Shock Delivery After Automated External Defibrillator Activation.
why: It pinpoints the biggest delay in AED shock delivery, so we can target training to improve survival in cardiac arrest.
findings: Pad‑application takes most of the time—median 42 s, about 81 % of the total 60‑s window. If pad‑application is done within 50 s, most shocks can be delivered within 60 s.
take_home: Aim to finish pad‑application in ≤50 s to hit the 60‑s shock‑delivery goal.

title: Association between burst-suppression with identical bursts and multimodal measures of cerebral oxygenation after cardiac arrest.
why: In post‑cardiac arrest patients, the EEG pattern BSIB signals a distinct brain‑injury phenotype that could affect ICU monitoring and care.
findings: BSIB was linked to higher jugular venous O₂ saturation, a lower CO₂ gap, and lower intracranial pressure, suggesting impaired oxygen metabolism but preserved delivery.
take_home: Recognizing BSIB on EEG may help identify patients with a specific cerebral oxygenation profile after cardiac arrest, guiding targeted monitoring.

title: Real-time feedback during bag-valve-mask ventilation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a before-and-after study (VEntilation during Cardiac Arrest Resuscitation Study, VECARS-2).
why: Good ventilation matters for post‑resuscitation care, so knowing if tech helps is useful for ICU teams.
findings: Real‑time feedback lowered the variability of delivered volume and reduced leak volume, but the actual tidal volume stayed about the same. About two‑thirds of breaths hit the target 400‑600 mL range with feedback versus 42 % without.
take_home: Real‑time feedback can tighten ventilation quality during CPR, but its impact on patient outcomes still needs confirmation.

title: Assessment of Tidal Volume in Patients Undergoing Noninvasive Ventilation: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
why: Because NIV is common in ICU and high tidal volume may predict failure and mortality, which matters for managing ARF in cardiac patients
findings: Higher Vt/PBW was linked to NIV failure, especially in hypoxemic ARF, and to higher mortality, higher respiratory rate and lower PaCO2, but not to pressure support levels
take_home: Watch tidal volume in NIV—elevated Vt/PBW signals higher risk of failure and worse outcomes, so consider tighter Vt control

title: Acute heart failure in emergency settings.
why: This consensus gives practical, evidence‑based guidance for ED management of acute heart failure, a common and high‑mortality presentation in the ICU.
findings: It stresses rapid phenotypic classification (decompensated HF, pulmonary oedema, RV failure, cardiogenic shock) to guide early treatment, reviews prehospital and ED evidence on biomarkers, imaging, ventilation, diuretics, vasodilators, and early GDMT, and highlights validated risk‑stratification tools.
take_home: Rapid phenotype‑based triage and early evidence‑based interventions in the ED can improve outcomes, but pragmatic trials are needed to refine prehospital and biomarker‑guided strategies.

title: Vascular Function and Cardiorespiratory Fitness in Adults Who Use Nicotine Vapes.
why: Early vascular dysfunction from vaping could foreshadow future cardiovascular events, so it matters for prevention strategies.
findings: Vape users had lower flow‑mediated dilation and carotid reactivity, and their peak oxygen uptake and cardiac output during exercise were reduced compared with non‑users.
take_home: Nicotine vaping in young adults is associated with early vascular and fitness impairments, hinting at a potential long‑term cardiovascular risk.

title: Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance Imaging in Cardio-Oncology: An Expert Consensus Statement from the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance. Endorsed by the International Cardio-Oncology Society (ICOS).
why: CMR gives detailed tissue insight for cancer patients, helping spot early heart damage before symptoms appear.
findings: The consensus outlines when to use CMR, how to time scans, and specific protocols for LV function, strain, myocardial injury, pericardial disease, iron overload, amyloidosis, and more.
take_home: In cardio‑oncology, CMR should be routinely used to detect subclinical cardiac injury and guide therapy decisions.

title: Specific effects of Pulsed Field Ablation on the cardiac tissue, the nervous system and the conduction system in experimental and clinical studies.
why: PFA is a new ablation tool that promises better tissue selectivity and fewer nerve complications, which is highly relevant for arrhythmia management.
findings: The review shows that PFA preferentially lesions myocardium while sparing nerves, with only rare permanent neural injury. Lesion formation differs from radiofrequency, with distinct maturation patterns. In fibrotic or fatty tissue, electric field distribution affects durability. Conduction system injury depends on field dose and proximity.
take_home: PFA offers a promising, tissue‑selective ablation with minimal nerve damage, but careful dose titration and awareness of conduction system proximity remain essential.

title: Safety considerations and clinical monitoring during pulsed field ablation.
why: PFA looks safer than thermal ablation, but you still need to watch for vasospasm and other quirks.
findings: PFA cuts classic thermal complications like pulmonary vein stenosis and phrenic nerve injury. It can cause coronary vasospasm, mild haemolysis, and silent brain lesions, and may briefly interfere with pacemakers or defibrillators.
take_home: Use PFA for arrhythmia ablation, but keep an eye on coronary anatomy, hydration, and device proximity to avoid vasospasm, haemolysis, and interference.

title: Pulsed field ablation: from concepts to technology.
why: PFA is a new ablation modality that could reduce collateral damage and improve safety in arrhythmia treatment.
findings: PFA relies on precise waveform parameters—monophasic vs biphasic, pulse width, duty cycle—to create lesions. Catheter design (bipolar vs monopolar) shapes the electric field and lesion geometry. Safety issues like Joule heating and device interference must be managed. Workflow and mapping integration are key for clinical adoption.
take_home: PFA shows promise as a safer, efficient arrhythmia ablation tool, but its success hinges on optimized waveforms, catheter design, and rigorous safety protocols.

title: Biophysical principles of pulsed field ablation.
why: PFA is a new non‑thermal ablation method that could change how we treat arrhythmias, so it’s worth knowing the science behind it.
findings: PFA uses pulsed electric fields to create irreversible electroporation, forming nanoscale pores in cell membranes when a threshold is exceeded. The size and permanence of these pores depend on pulse amplitude, duration, number, frequency, waveform, and tissue properties. Lesion formation is governed by both field intensity and exposure conditions, with reversible permeabilization possible if thresholds aren’t crossed.
take_home: PFA offers a promising, non‑thermal alternative for arrhythmia ablation, but more cardiomyocyte‑specific data are needed to optimize its safety and durability.

title: Treatment of paroxysmal and persistent atrial fibrillation with pulsed field ablation.
why: PFA looks like a safer, faster alternative to thermal ablation for AF, which could change how we manage patients in the cath lab.
findings: In paroxysmal AF, 12‑month freedom from arrhythmia is 75‑85 % with major complications <3 %. In persistent AF, freedom is 60‑75 % and complications stay below 3 %. PFA also reduces pain, analgesic use, and may allow same‑day discharge.
take_home: PFA offers comparable efficacy to thermal ablation but with fewer complications and a more patient‑friendly recovery, making it a compelling option for AF ablation.

title: Controlling pulsed field ablation efficacy during ablation procedures.
why: PFA is becoming a go‑to tool for arrhythmia ablation, so knowing what drives lesion success matters for outcomes.
findings: The review shows lesion size depends on electric field and exposure, not on thermal cues. Conventional markers like impedance or electrogram changes poorly predict durable lesions. Multiparametric models that combine electrical, mechanical, and positional data look promising in preclinical work, but clinical validation is still scarce.
take_home: Until we have reliable real‑time markers, we’ll keep relying on standardized energy protocols and good catheter positioning, while watching for emerging imaging and mapping tools that could make PFA more reproducible.

title: Sedation and anaesthesia in pulsed-field ablation for atrial fibrillation: mechanisms, procedural requirements, and real-world practice.
why: Because how you sedate patients during PFA can affect safety, workflow and recovery, which matters for every AF ablation you perform.
findings: Both deep sedation and general anaesthesia are safe and effective when monitored properly. Deep sedation can speed up workflow and improve recovery, especially with modern biphasic PFA systems that reduce muscle activation. General anaesthesia is still needed for complex cases or patients with high comorbidity. Practice varies widely across regions and centres.
take_home: Choose the sedation depth and anaesthesia type based on patient risk, procedural complexity and device characteristics, aiming for the lightest effective approach.

title: The future of PFA in cardiac ablation procedures.
why: PFA is a hot topic in arrhythmia ablation, and this review outlines its expanding uses and the gaps that still need to be addressed.
findings: The paper highlights that PFA is already feasible for linear atrial lesions, substrate modification, complex atrial tachycardias, and even ventricular arrhythmia ablation. It also points out that elderly patients and those at higher procedural risk may benefit from its favorable safety profile. However, the authors note that procedural endpoints and lesion durability are still poorly defined, and that standardised terminology is lacking across different commercial systems.
take_home: PFA looks promising beyond pulmonary vein isolation, but we need better endpoint definitions and durability data before it becomes a routine choice.

title: The perspective of combining pulsed field ablation and left atrial appendage closure.
why: It highlights that combining pulsed field ablation with left atrial appendage closure is still experimental and not yet proven superior to standard ablation plus anticoagulation.
findings: Current data come mainly from feasibility studies and early observations; no trial has shown that PFA‑LAAC beats radiofrequency or cryoballoon ablation. OAC‑withdrawal studies report low stroke rates in low‑risk patients, but caution is advised for older, frailer patients.
take_home: PFA‑LAAC may be an option for carefully selected patients, but it’s not yet a routine strategy and needs prospective trials to confirm benefit.

title: Long-term predictors of outcome in Brugada syndrome patients after implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implant.
why: Knowing which Brugada patients truly need an ICD can spare many from unnecessary shocks and guide follow‑up intensity.
findings: In a 551‑patient cohort, 11% had life‑threatening arrhythmias over 8.1 years. ESC class IIA patients had similar risk to those with secondary prevention. A 5‑year BrS risk score that includes genetics and ECG data distinguished those who did and did not experience events.
take_home: Apply the BrS risk score at the time of ICD implantation to better identify patients who will benefit from the device.

title: Scientific Output in Septic Shock According to Country Income and Gender: A Meta-Epidemiological Study.
why: It shows how research output in septic shock is skewed by country income and gender, which could affect the evidence base we rely on for critical care decisions.
findings: LMIC-affiliated first authors rose from 18% to 37% over a decade, women made up 35.6% of first authors and 25% of last authors—higher in LMICs than HICs. Female first authors were more likely to have female last authors, and cross‑income collaborations were rare. In HICs, male‑led papers appeared in higher‑impact journals, a gap not seen among LMIC authors.
take_home: Even with growing LMIC and female participation, significant inequities in authorship and journal impact remain—highlighting the need for more inclusive, collaborative research efforts.

title: Cluster Versus Individual Randomization in Prehospital, Emergency and Critical Care Trials: A Meta-Epidemiological Study.
why: It shows that the way trials are randomized can change the apparent benefit of treatments in emergency settings, which matters when we interpret ICU studies.
findings: The study found no difference in mortality estimates between cluster and individual randomization, but cluster trials reported smaller effect sizes for length‑of‑stay or days‑alive outcomes.
take_home: When reviewing ICU meta‑analyses, check whether cluster‑RCTs are mixed in, as they may underestimate treatment effects on time‑based outcomes.

title: Furosemide Stress Test in Adults and Children With Acute Kidney Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
why: AKI is common in ICU cardiology, and a bedside test could help us triage patients for dialysis.
findings: The furosemide stress test had moderate sensitivity and high specificity for predicting AKI progression and KRT initiation, but was less accurate for mortality. It did not improve short‑term mortality when used to guide early dialysis.
take_home: Use the FST to risk‑stratify AKI in ICU patients, but expect limited impact on survival.

title: Delay From Hypotension Onset to Appropriate Antifungal Therapy Initiation Is the Critical Determinant of Outcome in Candida Septic Shock.
why: Because septic shock can precipitate cardiogenic shock and ICU cardiologists often manage such patients, timing of therapy is critical.
findings: In 850 Candida septic shock patients, only 16.9% received pathogen‑appropriate antifungals within 6 h of hypotension. Each hour of delay raised the odds of death by 4.5 %. Survival was 86 % if therapy started within 2 h, then fell 5 % per hour thereafter.
take_home: Get the right antifungal in the first hours of hypotension—every hour matters for survival.

title: Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
why: Though not a cardiac study, it shows music therapy can lower sedation and tracheostomy rates in ICU patients, which may affect post‑ICU cardiac outcomes.
findings: Weaning duration was unchanged, but agitation and sedation scores improved, propofol use fell, and tracheostomy rates dropped. Pain and stress scores were not significantly different, and vital signs stayed stable.
take_home: Music therapy during ICU weaning may reduce agitation, sedation needs, and tracheostomy rates, but it does not shorten weaning or ICU stay.

title: Sex differences in cardiovascular disease burden, risk factors, and disease spectrum in Europe: a global burden of disease 2023 analysis within the ESC Atlas framework.
why: It shows that men and women in Europe carry the same overall CVD burden but in very different ways, so prevention plans need to be sex-specific.
findings: Women have a lower share of ischemic heart disease and a higher share of peripheral arterial disease. Men expose more to tobacco and alcohol, while women have higher BMI and less physical activity. Maternal hypertensive disorders account for a quarter of new CVD cases in women and vary hugely by country.
take_home: Tailor prevention to sex: cut tobacco/alcohol in men, tackle obesity and inactivity in women, and aggressively manage hypertensive disorders during pregnancy.

title: Advanced Subclinical Atherosclerosis in Young Individuals and Risk of Mortality Over 30 Years: The Coronary Artery Calcium Consortium.
why: Even though it’s a long‑term study, it shows that a high CAC score in people under 45 predicts future death, so we can spot high‑risk patients early.
findings: In a cohort of 12,847 young adults, those with CAC >90% had almost double the all‑cause mortality and more than triple the CHD mortality over 30 years compared with those with zero calcium.
take_home: A CAC score above 90% in a 30‑45‑year‑old flags a markedly higher long‑term risk, so consider aggressive prevention even in this age group.

title: Pacing Related Conduction Delay as an Indicator of Intramural Site of Origin of Focal Ventricular Arrhythmias.
why: It shows a simple pacing‑map metric that flags deeper intramural VAs, which can explain why some ablations fail.
findings: A mismatch >26 ms between the stimulus‑QRS and the local EGM‑QRS predicts ineffective ablation of a site that otherwise looks good on pace‑mapping. In the cohort, 8 of 9 such sites failed, but alternative deeper sites were successfully ablated in most patients.
take_home: If the S‑QRS/EGM‑QRS gap exceeds 26 ms, suspect an intramural origin and pursue further mapping before giving up on the initial site.

title: Safety and Outcomes of Transvenous Lead Extraction of Advisory ePTFE-Coated Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator Leads: A Multicenter Experience With RELIANCE G.
why: It shows that removing the advisory ePTFE‑coated ICD leads is safe and effective, so we can reassure patients and plan procedures accordingly.
findings: In 423 patients, 95.5% had complete lead removal and 98.8% clinical success, with only 0.9% major complications and 2.8% 30‑day mortality mainly in infection cases. Calcified leads didn’t raise complication rates.
take_home: Even with long dwell times and calcification, TLE of these leads is safe and successful at experienced centers.

title: The Vein of Marshall Promotes Re-Entry After Pulmonary Vein Reconnection.
why: It shows how the vein of Marshall can make post‑ablation atrial tachycardia more likely, which matters when deciding on ablation strategy.
findings: In simulated models, re‑entry happened in 31% of reconnection sites when the vein of Marshall was intact, dropping to 13% or 10% when it was disconnected. The risk difference was about 20 percentage points.
take_home: Targeting the vein of Marshall during pulmonary vein isolation may reduce the chance of recurrent atrial tachycardia.

title: Pulsed Field Ablation of the Left Atrial Appendage Before Mechanical Closure to Reduce Peri-Device Leak (STUN-AF).
why: It shows that pulsed‑field ablation of the left atrial appendage before closure can cut the common peri‑device leak problem in AF patients.
findings: In 317 patients, those who had LAAA had 29% vs 64% leak rates at 3‑4 months and 4% vs 42% at 12 months; device compression was higher but safety was unchanged.
take_home: Adding LAAA to LAAC may reduce leaks without extra risk.

title: Bromocriptine for Myocardial Recovery in Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: Design and Rationale of the REBIRTH Trial.
why: It’s a planned RCT that could change how we treat postpartum heart failure, a niche but important area for ICU cardiologists.
findings: The study will randomize 200 women with peripartum cardiomyopathy to bromocriptine or placebo on top of guideline‑directed therapy, measuring LVEF at 6 months as the primary outcome, with longer‑term follow‑up for survival and heart‑failure events.
take_home: No results yet—results expected in 2027, so keep an eye out for whether bromocriptine truly boosts recovery in PPCM.

title: Multidisciplinary Collaboration in the Performance of Aortic Surgery: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association.
why: It shows how teamwork among surgeons, anesthesiologists and perfusionists shapes aortic surgery outcomes, which matters for cardiologists involved in peri‑operative care.
findings: The statement highlights that each team member’s actions can immediately affect others, and that aortic surgery requires coordination around ventilation, cooling, and organ protection.
take_home: Successful aortic surgery hinges on clear multidisciplinary communication and shared protocols.

title: Sirolimus-Coated Balloon Angioplasty for Femoropopliteal Artery Disease Without Tissue Loss: A Secondary Analysis of the SirPAD Trial.
why: It’s a peripheral artery study, not directly in your cardiogenic shock or imaging focus, but it shows how drug-coated balloons can reduce revascularization in femoropopliteal disease.
findings: In patients without tissue loss, sirolimus-coated balloons cut 1‑year target‑lesion revascularization by about 10% versus uncoated balloons, and lowered major adverse limb events by roughly 5%. All‑cause death was similar.
take_home: Sirolimus-coated balloons may lower revascularization and limb complications in femoropopliteal disease, but the data are descriptive and not practice‑changing.

title: Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy Using a Conduction System Pacing Defibrillation Lead in Patients Meeting CRT-D Indications: Six-Month Clinical Outcomes Results From the ASCEND CSP Study.
why: It shows a new pacing method that works as well as, if not better than, the standard CRT, which could change how we treat patients with heart failure and ICDs.
findings: The study implanted a conduction‑system pacing ICD lead in 52 patients with a 98% success rate and 100% defibrillation success. QRS width narrowed by about 30 ms and LVEF rose by 10 points on average. Response rates were higher than with conventional biventricular pacing—71% responders and 34% super‑responders versus 49% and 8% in the matched cohort.
take_home: CSP ICD leads for CRT provide safe, effective pacing with superior LV remodeling and clinical response compared to traditional BiV‑CRT.

title: Assessment and Reversibility of Hepatic Abnormalities in Heart Failure: Liver in Heart Failure.
why: Liver dysfunction is common in advanced HF and can influence decisions about mechanical circulatory support and transplant timing.
findings: Hepatic injury stems from congestion and hypoperfusion; standard liver tests and imaging are limited in accuracy; cardiac function improvement often normalizes biochemistries, but histologic reversal is variable; severe fibrosis may warrant combined heart‑liver transplantation.
take_home: In advanced heart failure, liver disease is frequent and may improve with cardiac support, yet we lack reliable tools to assess severity or predict outcomes.

title: Cardiac Structure and Function in Women After Preeclampsia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
why: Preeclampsia can silently damage the heart for years, so knowing the long‑term risk helps us decide who needs follow‑up and maybe early therapy.
findings: Women who had preeclampsia show higher left‑ventricular mass and lower global longitudinal strain during pregnancy, and the strain remains reduced for up to 10 years after delivery. LV mass stays elevated postpartum, but other echo measures are similar to controls.
take_home: Preeclampsia leaves a lasting, subclinical myocardial scar that can persist for a decade—early, routine echo screening may catch it before overt heart failure develops.

title: Feasibility and Restenosis Predictors of Optical Frequency Domain Imaging-Guided Drug-Coated Balloon Treatment for Femoropopliteal Lesions.
why: It’s a peripheral‑vascular study, so not a core focus, but the imaging‑guided approach could inform how we think about intravascular imaging in other settings.
findings: OFDI‑guided drug‑coated balloon therapy worked well—about 92% procedural success and 85% were restenosis‑free at one year. A calcified nodule on OFDI was linked to higher restenosis risk.
take_home: OFDI can guide DCB treatment in selected femoropopliteal lesions, but calcified nodules raise the restenosis risk.

title: Myocardial Alterations in Major Depressive Disorder with Anxious Distress: Evidence from Oxygenation-Sensitive CMR and Entropy Analysis.
why: It shows that depression can alter myocardial tissue characteristics, which might be relevant when assessing cardiac risk in patients with mood disorders.
findings: Patients with major depressive disorder and anxious distress had higher myocardial entropy on T1 and T2 mapping and lower oxygenation-sensitive signal change compared with healthy controls. These changes correlated with depression and anxiety severity and with cardiovascular symptoms.
take_home: Oxygenation-sensitive CMR and entropy mapping could serve as noninvasive early markers of myocardial involvement in depressed patients, but their clinical utility in acute cardiac care remains to be established.

title: Short-term safety, feasibility, and performance of a novel soft robotic biventricular mechanical circulatory support device avoiding blood contact - The MISSION reBEAT trial.
why: This new soft‑robotic biventricular support avoids blood contact, potentially cutting complications in cardiogenic shock or advanced HF patients.
findings: In 10 patients the device was implanted in about 3 minutes, with only two minor procedure‑related events and no severe adverse events. Hemodynamics improved: MAP rose from ~67 to ~76 mmHg, stroke work and cardiac power output increased significantly. The system also showed no tissue injury or new ECG changes.
take_home: A promising, blood‑contact‑free biventricular MCS that is safe and hemodynamically beneficial in a small cohort, but larger trials are needed to confirm its role.

title: Association of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Radiographic Findings Identified by Machine Learning and Outcomes of Patients Receiving Invasive Mechanical Ventilation.
why: It shows a machine‑learning ARDS score can predict mortality and ventilator duration, which may help us decide who needs more aggressive care in the ICU.
findings: Among 6,591 ventilated patients, a positive ARDS-CXR score (>50% probability) was linked to 35% 28‑day mortality versus 13% for negative scores. The score’s AUROC for mortality was 0.68, slightly better than PaO2/FiO2. Each point increase in the score raised the risk of death and delayed extubation.
take_home: Consider incorporating ARDS-CXR scores into ICU triage to spot high‑risk patients early.

title: Brachial-to-Radial Pressure Gradient in Critically Ill Patients Treated With Vasoactive Agents: A Prospective Observational Study.
why: It shows that a sizable fraction of ICU patients on vasopressors have a measurable brachial‑radial pressure gap that correlates with higher drug doses and worse outcomes.
findings: About 18% of patients had a gradient >11 mmHg. Those patients needed more norepinephrine, had higher SOFA scores, longer capillary refill, and higher lactate. The gradient was independently linked to vasoactive dose and ICU mortality.
take_home: A significant brachial‑radial pressure gradient is common in vasopressor‑treated ICU patients and signals greater illness severity and higher mortality—monitor it and consider it when titrating vasoactive therapy.

title: Comparative Analysis of Tracheal Intubation-Associated Cardiac Arrest in 2015-2023: A Report From the National Emergency Airway Registry for Children Multicenter Registry.
why: TI‑CA is a real risk in pediatric ICUs, and airway choices can change that risk.
findings: About 1.2 % of intubations led to cardiac arrest. Shock or low oxygen before intubation, and each extra attempt, raised the odds. Using ketamine, propofol, neuromuscular blockers or video laryngoscopy lowered the odds, with video laryngoscopy partly helping by cutting down attempts.
take_home: Aim for first‑pass intubation with video laryngoscopy and agents like ketamine or propofol to keep TI‑CA rates low.

title: Clinical prediction models in cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
why: Knowing who’s at risk for kidney injury after cardiac surgery helps us target preventive measures and avoid dialysis.
findings: About a quarter of patients develop AKI, and 2% need dialysis. The Thakar 2005 score predicts dialysis‑requiring AKI with an AUC of 0.80, sensitivity 87% and specificity 49% at ≥3 points. Calibration tends to underestimate risk, and newer models like Demirjian 2022 look promising.
take_home: Use a validated score such as Thakar 2005 to flag high‑risk patients and apply early preventive strategies to reduce dialysis‑requiring AKI.

title: Mucormycosis in critically ill patients: a 9-year multicenter cohort study of clinical features, management, and 90-day outcomes.
why: Mucormycosis is a rare but deadly infection that can hit ICU patients, especially those with blood cancers or trauma, so knowing its risk factors and management can help us anticipate and treat it early.
findings: In 43 ICU patients, 90‑day mortality was 47%. Older age, hematologic malignancy, and higher SOFA score predicted death, while lower liposomal amphotericin B doses were linked to worse outcomes. Immune monitoring revealed low monocyte HLA‑DR in some patients, and interferon‑gamma therapy helped a few survive.
take_home: Early PCR‑based diagnosis, adequate amphotericin dosing, and immune monitoring—potentially with interferon‑gamma—may reduce mortality in ICU patients with mucormycosis.

title: Comparison of delivery room wrist versus earlobe pulse oximetry in newborns: A randomized controlled trial.
why: This study focuses on neonatal pulse oximetry, which is outside the cardiologist’s core interests.
findings: The earlobe probe had a shorter application time and reduced time from birth to a reliable signal compared with the wrist probe, but the time to reliable signal after probe placement was similar. Perfusion index was lower and reapplication rates higher with the earlobe probe.
take_home: Using an earlobe probe may speed initial signal acquisition in delivery rooms, but it does not improve the speed of obtaining a reliable reading once the probe is on.

title: Principles of drug dosing for obese patients in the intensive care unit.
why: Obesity is common in ICU and can alter drug PK/PD, so dosing matters for cardiology patients too.
findings: The review notes that product labels often ignore obesity-related PK changes, leading to potential treatment failure or toxicity. It stresses that individualized dosing—choosing the right weight metric and adjusting doses—is essential, but evidence is sparse and outcome data limited.
take_home: In obese ICU patients, tailor drug doses based on weight and PK considerations, and involve a pharmacist whenever possible.

title: Immediate Complete Revascularization During Index Admission in Older Patients With ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction.
why: Older STEMI patients with multivessel disease might fare worse if you rush to complete revascularization during the same admission.
findings: In patients 70 and older, immediate complete revascularization led to a higher rate of death, MI or revascularization compared with staged procedures. In younger patients the two strategies performed similarly.
take_home: For patients over 70 with STEMI and multivessel disease, consider staging the non‑culprit artery PCI rather than doing it immediately.

title: Earlier Versus Later Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Sequential Landmark Target Trial Emulation.
source: Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care
why: ECPR timing matters for refractory OHCA survival, and early initiation improves outcomes even beyond 60 minutes.
findings: In a Korean nationwide registry, patients who received ECPR within 15 minutes had 31% 30‑day survival versus 16% without ECPR; at 30 minutes survival was 21.6% vs 7.2%; even at 60 minutes survival was 10.9% vs 3.2%. Neurological outcomes followed the same trend.
take_home: Start ECPR as early as possible in refractory OHCA; the 60‑minute cutoff may be too conservative.

title: Role of Mitochondrial Impairment in Sepsis-Induced Platelet Activation.
why: Sepsis can trigger platelet hyperactivation that worsens organ injury—something we see in ICU patients—so understanding mitochondrial links is useful.
findings: Septic plasma impairs platelet mitochondrial respiration and Complex I activity, boosting platelet activation; the mitochondria‑targeted antioxidant MitoTEMPO reverses these changes in vitro.
take_home: Targeting platelet mitochondria with antioxidants like MitoTEMPO could blunt sepsis‑related platelet dysfunction and organ damage.
